items.title: Willis's 'lads'
items.claim: Paul Willis's Learning to Labour (1977) studied working-class boys in a Midlands school. What did he argue they were doing through their counter-school culture?

options.text: Actively rejecting school in ways that prepared them for manual labour

items.reveal_title: Resistance that reproduced the very inequality it opposed
items.reveal:
Willis combined Marxist theory with ethnography to argue the 'lads' partially saw through school ideology but their rejection led them into the same factory jobs their fathers held.

The study influenced both education research and cultural studies.
items.why: Ethnographic fieldwork can reveal mechanisms of class reproduction invisible in statistics.

items.title: Moral panics
items.claim: Stanley Cohen's Folk Devils and Moral Panics (1972) studied which group?

options.text: Mods and rockers at English seaside resorts in 1964

items.reveal_title: Bank holiday disturbances at Clacton and Brighton
items.reveal:
Cohen analysed how relatively minor incidents in 1964 were amplified by press coverage, generating reactions out of proportion to the original events.

The model has since been applied to repeated panics around drugs, immigration and youth culture.
items.why: Cohen's framework still organises how sociologists study media-driven public reactions.

items.title: The Chicago School's method
items.claim: Robert Park and the Chicago School in the 1920s pioneered which approach to studying social life?

options.text: Urban ethnography, mapping the city as a social laboratory

items.reveal_title: The city itself as a research site
items.reveal:
Park urged students to study the 'gold coast and the slum' through direct observation. The result included Wirth's Ghetto (1928), Anderson's The Hobo (1923) and Whyte's Street Corner Society (1943).

The school established urban sociology as a recognised field.
items.why: Method choice shapes what counts as evidence and what kind of theory is possible.
